subject: inflation
title: Why Your Dollar Shrinks
summary: Inflation, purchasing power, the CPI basket, and why a little inflation differs from a lot.

keys.prompt: What is inflation, and what happens to purchasing power when it rises?
keys.answer: Inflation is a general upward movement in prices. As prices rise, each dollar buys fewer goods and services—purchasing power falls.

keys.prompt: How is inflation measured with a "basket"?
keys.answer: A price index like the CPI tracks the average change in prices of a market basket of consumer goods and services over time.

keys.prompt: Why does the Fed aim for about 2% inflation, not zero?
keys.answer: The FOMC judges that 2% longer-run inflation (PCE) best fits price stability and maximum employment; low, stable inflation helps people plan saving, borrowing, and investment.

cards.title: The raise that wasn't
cards.text: Say you get a 2% raise, but prices rise 5% the same year. The paycheck looks bigger, yet it buys about 3% less. That gap—nominal dollars versus what they purchase—is purchasing power.

cards.question: If only gasoline jumps this month and food, rent, and clothes barely move, is that the same thing as "inflation"?

options.text: Yes — any price jump equals inflation
Not by itself — inflation is a general rise across the price level
Only if the Fed announces it on TV

cards.reveal: The Fed: inflation cannot be measured by one product or even several. It is a general increase in the overall price level.

cards.title: Definition, cleanly
cards.text: Inflation is a general upward movement in prices of goods and services over time. When the general price level rises, each unit of currency buys fewer goods and services. That loss is a drop in purchasing power.
cards.example: Investor.gov: inflation reduces purchasing power—a risk if you earn a fixed rate of interest while prices climb.

cards.title: The CPI basket
cards.text: A consumer price index (CPI) estimates the price level of a market basket of goods and services households buy. Statisticians weight items by how much people spend on them, then track how the basket's cost changes. The annual percent change is a common inflation rate.
cards.example: In the U.S., the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the CPI. The Fed also watches other indexes, including the PCE price index.

why.q: Why weight housing more heavily than, say, pencils?
why.a: A price index weights items by their share of typical spending, so big-budget categories move the overall measure more.

examples_by_interest.business: Say… your golf-ball resale side hustle tracks balls, shipping, and packaging as a mini basket. If that whole set rises 4% while you still charge last year's price, your real margin shrinks.
examples_by_interest.soccer: Say… a travel-team budget tracks fees, cleats, and snacks as a basket. If that basket rises faster than fundraising, the same dollar covers less of the season.
examples_by_interest.golf: Say… you track range fees, balls, and a lesson as a basket. A 3% rise in that basket means the same allowance buys slightly fewer rounds.

cards.title: Mild vs high
cards.text: Mild, steady inflation is different from high or wild inflation. High inflation makes planning hard, erodes cash holdings, and can scramble contracts. Most mainstream economists favor a low, steady rate rather than zero or a free-for-all.
cards.example: The Fed aims for 2% inflation over the longer run (PCE). It says when people expect inflation to stay low and stable, they can make sound decisions on saving, borrowing, and investment.

cards.title: Who feels it differently
cards.text: Unexpected inflation redistributes. Someone holding cash or owed a fixed dollar amount loses purchasing power. Someone who borrowed at a fixed interest rate may repay with dollars that buy less—so the real burden of the debt can fall. That is a description of the math, not a cheer for high inflation.
cards.example: Investor.gov flags inflation risk for people receiving a fixed rate of interest. The mirror image: fixed-rate borrowers can see the real cost of repayment ease when inflation runs hotter than expected.

cards.question: If your first job pays a fixed hourly wage for a year, what would you watch besides the dollar amount on the paycheck?
nudges: Think about what that wage buys: food, gear, phone plan.
How is that different from a wage that rises with a price index?

options.text: The same dollar buys fewer goods and services
options.why: Yes. That is the flip side of a rising general price level.
Sales lower prices. Inflation is about prices rising in general.

options.text: You switch from cash to a debit card
options.why: Payment method is not purchasing power.
Basket updates improve measurement; they are not the definition of falling purchasing power.

questions.q: What does the CPI mainly track?

options.text: Average price change for a market basket of consumer goods and services
options.why: Right. It is a weighted basket measure.
CPI is about consumer prices, not equities.

options.text: How many dollars are printed each day
options.why: Money supply is related in theory, but CPI measures prices paid.

questions.q: Why does the Fed target about 2% inflation over the longer run?

options.text: It judges 2% (PCE) most consistent with price stability and maximum employment
options.why: That is the FOMC's stated longer-run goal.

options.text: Because Congress bans any other number
options.why: The 2% figure is the FOMC's judgment in its longer-run goals statement.
2% a year is mild, not a doubling.

options.text: To make cash worthless on purpose
options.why: The aim is low, stable inflation so people can plan.
